analysis.one_liner: Gives the FTC power to win refunds and profit disgorgement from companies that scam consumers, and lets the Justice Department sue monopolies on behalf of consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill would have let the FTC win refunds for scam victims and let the Justice Department sue monopolies on consumers' behalf, but it died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the FTC's power to get money back for cheated consumers: courts could order companies that used deceptive practices to pay restitution, cancel unfair contracts, give refunds, and hand over profits made from the scam. It also would have let the Justice Department sue companies that violate antitrust laws on behalf of all U.S. residents harmed by the conduct, rather than requiring each person to sue alone. In exchange, it set specific rules: the FTC would have to prove consumers actually relied on the deception and were harmed, claims generally had to be brought within three years, and any disgorgement would be capped and offset against restitution.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers cheated by fraudulent or deceptive business practices would gain a way to get their money back through court-ordered refunds, rescission, and disgorgement, without hiring their own lawyer. People injured by monopolistic practices would benefit because the Justice Department could sue on their behalf collectively and recover damages plus attorneys' fees.

how_it_helps.text: Lets the FTC ask courts for refunds, restitution, contract cancellation, and return of property when companies cheat consumers through unfair or deceptive practices.
Lets the FTC seek disgorgement — forcing a company to give up the profits it made from the deception.
Adds a 3-year window to bring these claims, with the clock paused while the wrongdoer is outside the United States, so offshore scammers cannot simply wait it out.

Allows the Attorney General to sue antitrust violators on behalf of all U.S. residents, recovering damages and attorneys' fees for people injured by monopolistic conduct, without each consumer having to file an individual lawsuit.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that engage in deceptive practices would pay refunds, contract unwinding, and disgorgement of the profits they made from the violation; firms that violate antitrust laws would face federal damage suits brought on behalf of all injured U.S. residents.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the bar for consumer redress: courts could order restitution only where the FTC proves a reasonable person would have known the practice was deceptive, actually relied on it, and was harmed by it, and the law may not presume reliance merely from exposure to the practice.
Relief is time-limited: claims for restitution and disgorgement must generally be brought within 3 years of the violation, which could cut off recovery in long-running fraud schemes.
Disgorgement is capped at net profits directly related to the violation and offset by any restitution paid, so a company's total payout is limited even when consumer losses were larger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — giving the FTC real power to make cheated consumers whole and letting the Justice Department sue monopolists on behalf of ordinary Americans — is real and substantial. The bill balances it with genuine due-process safeguards (a demonstrated reliance requirement, a 3-year window, offsets to avoid double recovery), which is a fair design compromise, though those same limits would let some sophisticated scammers escape liability. The main weakness is not the design but the fate: it was never seriously advanced, so consumers got none of the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended — it never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 30, 2023, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the last action of its kind ever taken on it.
No further action was recorded through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that engage in consumer fraud and monopolistic practices are better off, because the stronger remedies were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that deceive consumers and monopolies

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its text giving the FTC restitution, refund, rescission, and disgorgement authority and the Justice Department parens patriae antitrust authority.

for.name: Sens. Ted Cruz, Josh Hawley, and Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans, but the bill never advanced far enough for anyone to vote on it, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Companies that profit from deceptive practices and fraud schemes
industries.note: The bill exposes them to court-ordered refunds, rescission, and disgorgement of profits under FTC enforcement, and to a longer enforcement reach against offshore operators.
The Justice Department could aggregate all U.S. residents' antitrust injuries into one federal suit with treble-style damages and attorneys' fees, raising the cost of monopolistic conduct.
